If you're retired, at this stage of the year, you may be eager to prepare yourself financially for 2027. Part of that means planning for your upcoming cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, if you're on Social Security. The Social Security Administration recently announced that benefits will be getting a 3.6% COLA in 2027. That should cause the average monthly retirement benefit to increase from $2,095 to $2,170. But a generous Social Security COLA could also have implications for the program's finances on a broad level, so it's important to know what a larger raise might mean for future benefits. Read More Here › SPONSORED How the 2027 Social Security COLA affects benefits and program revenue Social Security COLAs are designed to help benefits keep up with inflation. They're based on the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), which measures changes to the costs incurred by workers. A large Social Security COLA technically strains the program's financial resources. But that can't be helped, since COLAs need to match inflation, which has been rampant this year. On the flip side, in 2027, Social Security's wage cap is increasing. The wage cap is the amount of money that is taxed each year to fund Social Security. Payroll taxes are the program's main source of revenue. Next year, the Social Security wage cap will increase from $184,500 to $192,300. That added revenue should at least somewhat offset the upcoming COLA. Shopping for cheaper auto insurance? Enter your zip code here to get started. A large COLA isn't the reason Social Security faces sweeping benefit cuts If you've been paying attention to the news on Social Security, you may be aware that the program is facing some serious financial difficulties. The most recent report by the Social Security Trustees said that the program's Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund is expected to run out of money by the final quarter of 2032. Once that happens, Social Security can still pay benefits due to collecting future tax revenue. But a broad 22% cut to benefits may become necessary absent a fix from Congress. Now Congress could vote to merge Social Security's OASI Trust Fund with its Disability Insurance Trust Fund. Combined, the two funds would be able to pay 100% of benefits through 2034, after which benefits would potentially be looking at a 17% cut. Even with a merger of both funds, Social Security would face a 75-year actuarial deficit of about 4.42% of taxable payroll. In 2021, Social Security began tapping its trust fund to help pay for benefits. The reason the program has been in that position is that labor force participation rates have shrunk, depriving Social Security of key revenue it needs to stay afloat. In 1955, there were 8.8 workers per Social Security OASI beneficiary. That ratio fell to just 3.0 in 2025. While a large COLA in 2027 might seem to be something that will make Social Security's financial situation worse, it can't be helped. That 3.6% COLA is not a benefit expansion. It's a mandated adjustment to benefits based on recent inflation. The primary driver of Social Security cuts is a shrinking labor force, not the 2027 COLA, or any other COLA for that matter. Could raising the Social Security wage cap prevent future benefit cuts? Given that Social Security is facing broad benefit cuts, some lawmakers want to see the Social Security wage cap lifted or even eliminated. The logic is that making more wages subject to taxes could directly increase revenue for Social Security. A higher wage cap wouldn't change the COLA formula, though. And if inflation continues to surge, the program would still owe seniors large increases to ensure that their benefits don't fall behind. Learn More Here › SPONSORED How changing the Social Security COLA formula could affect future benefits The CPI-W has long been criticized by advocates as an imperfect formula for calculating COLAs. The reason is that it measures the costs incurred by wage earners. But retirees tend to spend their money differently. The nonpartisan Senior Citizens League wants to change the basis of COLAs to the Consumer Price Index for the Elderly (CPI-E). That way, COLAs can be based on seniors' real-world costs. The group says the CPI-E regularly puts spending inflation for seniors at two-tenths of a percentage point higher than the rate at which the CPI-W increases. That could lead to larger COLAs over time. However, a broad change to the COLA formula could also push Social Security closer to insolvency unless Congress simultaneously makes changes to boost program revenue. Bottom line Social Security is one of the most important benefits for seniors today. Without those monthly checks, many older Americans would struggle to cover their costs, so the idea of benefit cuts may be scary. The reality is that a large 2027 COLA isn't the reason Social Security faces broad benefit cuts. But a large COLA at any given point in time technically strains the program's limited resources. And a formula change that results in larger COLAs could bring Social Security closer to benefit cuts.  For this reason, it's important to pay attention to updates and see what lawmakers are discussing in the context of Social Security.
